text.p: Australasian food group Goodman Fielder Ltd announced the sale of its European milling and baking arm on Friday and reaffirmed it was on track for double-digit full year profit growth.
Net profit for the six months to December 31 rose 22 percent to A$55.9 million from A$45.9 previously, although much of the gain was due to lower abnormal items.
Pre-abnormal net profit rose 4.9 percent and Goodman Fielder said it was "not uncomfortable" with full-year pre-abnormal net profit predictions of A$115 million, a rise of about 14 percent.
Chief executive David Hearn said the company had turned in a solid performance in the half despite record wheat prices, which hurt the milling and baking and European units.

"All our other businesses showed significant improvements in their profitability which is an encouraging reflection that the actions were have taken are beginning to show through," he told a media briefing. Hearn said the European milling and baking business, Meneba NV, would be sold to Dutch-based CVC Capital Partners BV for slightly more than A$300 million.
The company also announced the purchase of the New Zealand milling and baking operations of Brisbane-based Defiance Mills Ltd for NZ$48 million.
Goodman believed Meneba would have required significant funds to grow, while it could generate few synergies between the European and Australian milling baking businesses, Hearn said.
The funds from the sale would initially be used to reduce debt, cutting gearing from 49 percent to near 20 percent.
Goodman Fielder would then concentrate on developing its business, with the near term focus on Australia and New Zealand.
"I think the Defiance acquisition is the perfect model for the sort of thing we have in mind," said Hearn, adding that it would allow Goodman to consolidate its position in New Zealand.
"We will be concentrating more, if not exclusively, on our Australasian portfolio to start with, with a view to expanding out from there," he said.
The first half pre-abnormals improvement resulted mainly from lower debt and interest payments.
Earnings before interest and tax were steady at A$121.5, but individual business units showed wide swings due to the impact of higher wheat prices.

Hearn said he expected a stronger second half as lower wheat prices flowed through to the milling and baking business, which recorded a 28 percent fall in first half earnings before interest and tax (EBIT).
Milling and baking would show a strong turnaround, ending the full year with an EBIT near the 1995/96 result of A$81.1 million, he said.
The edible oils division, which increased earnings 23 percent in the first half, would have a weaker second half due to higher oil prices and a weaker Australian dollar.
Goodman Fielder shares were up one cent at A$1.61 at 0330 GMT (2.30 p.m.).
